sections.body_en:
It is a positive mitzva to rest in the seventh year from working the land, as it is said (Vayikra 25:1-5): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe on Mount Sinai, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall rest a Sabbath to the Lord. Six years you shall sow your field, and six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its produce. But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the Lord… it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land."

The Torah further added four negative mitzvot, which forbid four kinds of work, and these are: sowing and pruning, reaping and grape-harvesting. As it is said (there 4-5): "You shall not sow your field and you shall not prune your vineyard. That which grows of itself from your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of your untended vine you shall not gather; it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land."

Two of these kinds of work concern making the produce grow: sowing is work in the field, and pruning is work on the tree. And two of them concern gathering the produce: reaping is gathering grain and the other field crops, and grape-harvesting is gathering grapes and the fruit of the tree. In this chapter we will deal with the two kinds of work meant to make the produce grow, and with the derivative kinds of work that stem from them, whose prohibition is rabbinic. In the next chapter we will deal with the two kinds of work meant to gather the produce.

The Sages said that the Torah could have mentioned only the work of sowing, and from it we would have learned its derivative, which is pruning, since it too helps the produce grow. And likewise it could have sufficed with mentioning the work of reaping, and from it we would have learned its derivative, which is grape-harvesting, since it too concerns picking produce. But the Torah specified two primary kinds of work and two derivatives, in order to teach us that only these four kinds of work are forbidden by a Torah negative prohibition, and these are: a) sowing (below 4). b) pruning, which includes any trimming that helps the produce grow (below 5).
c) reaping, which includes picking all kinds of field crops. d) grape-harvesting, which includes picking all kinds of tree fruit (below 3:3). One who transgresses one of these four kinds of work is liable to lashes by Torah law. But one who does one of their derivatives, that is, other kinds of work that help the produce of fields and trees grow, such as fertilising, clearing stones and hoeing, does not transgress a Torah negative prohibition; but the Sages made a fence for the Torah and forbade them. And everything we have learned, that these kinds of work are forbidden rabbinically, is on condition that they were done occasionally; but one who does them regularly, as a person works his field in all the years, although he did not transgress a negative prohibition, has cancelled a positive Torah mitzva, for he cancelled the mitzva to rest from the work of the field.1

notes_en.en:
In the laws of Shabbat there are thirty-nine primary kinds of work, and every derivative of a primary kind is forbidden by Torah law like the primary one. For example, 'sowing' is a primary kind of work, and its derivatives are: pruning, fertilising, watering, and anything that helps the plant grow. And likewise 'reaping' is a primary kind of work, and its derivatives are grape-harvesting or picking any kind of fruit, branch or leaf. By contrast, regarding Shevi'it we find that the Torah forbade only four kinds of work; and not only that, but pruning is a derivative of sowing, and grape-harvesting is a derivative of reaping. The Sages learned from this that in the laws of Shevi'it only the kinds of work the Torah listed are forbidden by Torah law and one who transgresses them receives lashes; and the Sages decreed and forbade their derivatives, and one who transgresses them receives rabbinic lashes. So it was ruled as halakha, following Rava (Mo'ed Katan 2b-3a; Rambam, Shemita 1:2-4). And Abaye holds that all the derivatives are forbidden by Torah law, following the plain meaning of the baraita in the Gemara there (Mo'ed Katan there). However, one who does the work of the field in his usual way as in all the years, even though he did not do one of the four kinds of work, has cancelled a positive Torah mitzva, as it is said (Vayikra 25:4-5): "But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the Lord… it shall be a year of solemn rest for the land" (Ramban, Vayikra 23:24; Ritva, Rosh Ha-Shana 32b. And Maran the Rav expanded on this in Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:4; Kuntres Aḥaron 7. And in Kuntres Aḥaron 2:2 he explained that so it is implied in the words of the Rambam 1:1; 1:4).
Accordingly, the words of Rabbi Akiva in the Mishna (Shevi'it 1:4) are understood, that there is a Torah mitzva to rest from ploughing in Shevi'it, as it is said (Shemot 34:21): "In ploughing time and in harvest you shall rest." And this is difficult, for ploughing is not one of the four kinds of work forbidden by a negative prohibition; but one who ploughs regularly has cancelled a positive Torah mitzva (and see below in note 7). And one may understand from this that anyone who does one of the derivatives regularly, as in all the years, if he took great trouble over it, has cancelled a positive Torah mitzva. The Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:3 wrote similarly.

sections.title_en: 2. Sustaining and Improving – Okmei and Avruyei
sections.body_en:
This is the rule: work meant to make the produce of the field grow or to improve it is forbidden, and it is called work of 'avruyei' (improving). And work meant to sustain the trees so that they do not die or become damaged is permitted, and it is called 'okmei' (sustaining). For the aim of the mitzva is not that every seven years all the trees should die and after Shevi'it the whole orchard would have to be planted anew; rather the intention is that Israel should rest from work meant to make the produce grow and to improve the trees.

All the kinds of work forbidden by a Torah negative prohibition are always forbidden in the shemita, for the kinds of work the Torah mentioned are not meant to sustain the trees but to grow produce and gather it. Sowing makes new produce grow, and pruning causes the trees to produce more and better fruit. And even in our time, when shemita is rabbinic, the kinds of work the Torah forbade are always forbidden. And the other kinds of field work, which are forbidden rabbinically, are sometimes meant for making the produce grow and improving it, and sometimes meant for sustaining the trees. For growing and improving it is forbidden to do them, and for sustaining it is permitted to do them. However, many times, when one does work to sustain the tree, there is also benefit from it for its growth. But as long as the main aim is to sustain the tree, and without this aim one would not do this action, the action is permitted even though there is also a side benefit from it for the growth of the tree.

In the following halakhot we will explain the kinds of work forbidden by Torah law and those forbidden rabbinically. And although today the mitzva of Shevi'it with all its prohibitions is rabbinic, one must know what was forbidden at its root by Torah law, for the whole permission to do work to sustain the trees applies only to those kinds of work that are forbidden rabbinically.2

notes_en.en:
There are Rishonim from whom one could understand that even the Torah-level work of pruning is permitted for okmei (see Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:20). On the other hand, some say that all the kinds of work forbidden rabbinically are permitted for sustaining only on condition that they do not touch the tree itself (Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20, se'if katan 11; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:6-7). But the view of the great majority of poskim is that the Torah-level kinds of work are always forbidden, and the rabbinic kinds of work, when they are for okmei, are permitted even when they touch the tree (Mo'ed Katan 2b; Rambam 1:10; Semag; Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:5, 8; and note 44). When we look closely we find that the four kinds of work forbidden by Torah law are always meant for making the produce grow and gathering it, and never for sustaining the tree. And this is the foundation for understanding the difference between pruning, which is forbidden in every situation, and the kinds of trimming permitted for sustaining. For the pruning forbidden by Torah law is that done at the place that helps the growth of the tree in order to improve the produce, whereas other trimmings are actions that sometimes are meant for making the produce grow and sometimes for sustaining the tree (and see below 5, note 6).
However, one should know that usually actions meant for okmei also help avruyei; for if one fertilises a plant, for example, so that it will not wither, in practice it will also continue to grow. And if one trims branches to prevent diseases or to ensure its survival for many years, the growth in the branches afterwards will increase; and nevertheless it is permitted (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 11). This is the rule: any action whose main aim is okmei, and without this aim one would not do it, even when incidentally it helps avruyei, there is no prohibition in it. (And see below in note 6 on the question of pesik reisha.)

sections.title_en: 3. The Definitions of Sustaining the Tree and Sustaining the Fruit
sections.body_en:
Since it is a mitzva to rest in the seventh year from the work of the field and the tree, and the whole permission to do work to sustain the trees is only for lack of choice, to prevent damage, therefore one must do all possible preparatory actions before the seventh year begins, in order to reduce as much as possible the actions of sustaining in Shevi'it. And the same law applies to kinds of work that need to be done to sustain the trees towards the end of the shemita year: if it is possible to postpone doing them until after the shemita without damage being caused to the trees, one is obligated to postpone. And it seems that one who was negligent and did not prepare his field properly before the shemita must ask a Torah scholar whether he may do in the shemita the kinds of work he could have done before the shemita; for perhaps by being negligent he showed that such a loss is not important to him, and he has no permission to do it (see Peninei Halakha, Festivals 12:3, on the law of one who deliberately times his work for the festival).

It is permitted to do kinds of work forbidden rabbinically in order to save trees and perennial plants from death, or in order to prevent significant damage to them, for example that the amount of fruit they will yield in the eighth year will decrease significantly. Therefore it is permitted to water the trees so that they will not die or wither; and likewise it is permitted to remove diseased branches from the trees so that they do not infect the whole tree; and likewise it is permitted to spray the tree in order to destroy pests and prevent diseases. And likewise it is permitted to spray the ground with germination inhibitors or herbicides, in order to prevent the spread of weeds such as Bermuda grass; for otherwise, in the eighth year they would need to invest many resources in cleaning and fertilising the ground. This permission applies also when it is a concern of damage, on condition that the concern is reasonable and farmers are always accustomed to take trouble to prevent it (Ma'amar Mordekhai 3:12; see Peninei Halakha, Festivals 12:2, on situations of doubt).

The permission for these kinds of work is only in order to sustain the trees, so that no damage is caused to them that would require great trouble or great expense to restore in the eighth year; but it is forbidden to do kinds of work that are forbidden rabbinically in order to make the produce of Shevi'it grow or to sustain it. For this produce is ownerless, and the owner of the field may not take trouble for it. And some are lenient to do kinds of work forbidden rabbinically in order to make the fruit grow, so that the yield of the tree will be close to its yield in all the years. And although several poskim of our generation inclined to this permission, it is very hard to accept it. And Maran Rav Kook zt"l ruled that the permission for these kinds of work is only for sustaining the tree and the land, and in no way for the fruit. And it is clear that the 'heter mekhira' is more broad-based than this strained permission; therefore one who does not want to let his field lie fallow should use the 'heter mekhira' and not do work to sustain the fruit.3

notes_en.en:
According to the Ḥazon Ish (16:4; 21:14) and Rav Tikochinsky (Sefer Ha-Shemita 4:2, note 5), sustaining the fruit too is considered 'okmei', and therefore it is permitted to do rabbinic kinds of work in order to sustain the fruit yield in the shemita. And the Ḥazon Ish based his words on the permission to water in Shevi'it for the sake of produce, as they said in the baraita (Mo'ed Katan 6b): "One may water a grain field in Shevi'it so that vegetables will come up after Shevi'it." And likewise they said (Mishna Shevi'it 2:10): "One may mix [water and earth] around rice in Shevi'it"; mixing is combining the water with the earth in which the rice grows. And likewise (there 2:2): "Rabbi Shimon says: one may even remove the leaf from the cluster in Shevi'it," and their view is like those who hold that the first Tanna does not disagree with Rabbi Shimon (Gra); thus it is permitted to do rabbinic work for the sake of sustaining the fruit. And they inferred this from more places. Also Minḥat Shlomo 3:132; Ma'amar Mordekhai 3:8-9; Shevitat Ha-Sadeh 6:5, note 5, agreed with the view of the Ḥazon Ish. And my teacher and master Rav Yisraeli (Ḥavat Binyamin 3:103) agreed to permit work for sustaining fruit that has already begun to grow, so that it will grow reasonably, for there is holiness in it and it is forbidden to destroy it, but not for fruit that has not yet grown. In practice, those who follow the Ḥazon Ish permitted in his name any work to prevent a significant decrease in the quantity or quality of the fruit, and some explained that the intention is to prevent damage of about a sixth of the quantity or quality of the yield (see Mishpetei Eretz 3, note 5). But Maran Rav Kook ruled that the permission for rabbinic kinds of work for okmei is only for sustaining the tree for the following years, and in no way for the fruit of the shemita, because it is ownerless and the owner of the field has no connection to it, and therefore its loss need not concern him. And what they permitted, to water a grain field and to mix around rice, is to prevent loss after Shevi'it. And the permission to remove the leaf that harms the cluster is for fruit of the sixth year that continued to grow in Shevi'it, or to prevent damage to the tree (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:5, 16; 1:15, 4; Kuntres Aḥaron 12; Mishpat Kohen 79). And so wrote Torat Ha-Shevi'it p. 43; Devar Ha-Shemita p. 58. And so it emerges from the words of Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20:4.
And one must say as Maran the Rav, for it is explained in the Mishnayot of Shevi'it chapters 2-4, and in the baraita (Mo'ed Katan 3a), that in Shevi'it it is forbidden to weed, to hoe, to cut grass, to trim, to thin, to strip, to fertilise, to remove leaves, to dust, to smoke, and to make hollows around the vines. And if okmei of the fruit were permitted, many of these kinds of work would be needed in Shevi'it; for if, for example, one does not fertilise or hoe, it is clear that the fruit yield will be significantly harmed and will be very far from the yield of the other years. And not only that, but the Sages forbade clearing out manure and keeping animals in one's field lest he appear as one fertilising his field (Mishna Shevi'it 3:1-4); thus it was clear that there is no permission to fertilise fields for the sake of sustaining the fruit, for if there were permission, there would have been no need to decree absolutely because of appearances, since many times this is needed for okmei of the fruit. And so it is proven from the fact that the Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not mention the concept 'okmei of the fruit', nor did they discuss it in practice; and how could they have ignored one of the most practical subjects in Shevi'it? Admittedly, one could argue that in the agriculture of our time the trees produce much more fruit, and consequently the lack of care for them is more significant today. But still one must say that also in the past fertilising, hoeing and the like helped the fruit yield greatly, and refraining from them created a significant decrease in the fruit yield, and we have not heard that they permitted fertilising and hoeing for sustaining the fruit. And so one must understand from the mitzva of the Torah itself, which forbade sowing fields, so that there would be no field crops at all. Consequently it is clear that regarding the tree too, the fruit is that which will grow by itself, and not that work will be done for it.
And perhaps they came to permit okmei of the fruit out of a conception that the aim of the shemita is to give produce to all the inhabitants of the land. But the aim is to rest, as is explicit in the Torah; and only after one rests, regarding the fruit of the tree that grows by itself, are there warnings. And it is reasonable that many accepted this strained permission because they did not want to accept the 'heter mekhira', which according to the law is much more broad-based than it.

sections.body_en:
Included in the mitzva of shemita is not to sow in Shevi'it, as it is said (Vayikra 25:4): "You shall not sow your field." The Torah prohibition of sowing includes sowing kinds of grain, legumes and vegetables, and any seed or seedling that will produce fruit (see below 3:6). Even in order to practise the work of sowing or to check whether the seeds are good, it is forbidden to sow seeds in the ground.

Regarding planting a tree, the poskim disagree. Some say that just as sowing grain and vegetables is forbidden by Torah law, so planting a fruit tree is forbidden by Torah law. And so one can learn by a kal va-ḥomer: if pruning a tree, which improves its growth, is forbidden by Torah law, all the more so planting it is forbidden by Torah law (R. Shimshon and Rash Sirillo). But in the view of many, planting is forbidden only rabbinically (Rambam 1:4; Rabbeinu Tam; Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan). And this is because the kinds of work forbidden by a Torah negative prohibition concern making produce grow in the coming season; and therefore there are two prohibitions: one who sows annual crops, or one who prunes, for by these one makes produce grow. But one who plants a tree will receive fruit only after several years, and therefore there is no negative prohibition in it (Mahari"t Tzahalon, new responsa 176). However, we have already learned that one who does the work of his field in Shevi'it regularly cancels a positive Torah mitzva.4

Just as it is forbidden to plant a tree, so it is forbidden to graft one tree onto another, and likewise it is forbidden to layer a tree, that is, to take a branch and pass it through the ground so that another tree will grow from it (Rambam 1:4).

If a person transgressed and planted a tree in Shevi'it, the Sages penalised him that he must uproot the tree he planted. And they were stricter in Shevi'it than on Shabbat; for on Shabbat they penalised only one who planted deliberately, that he must uproot, but in Shevi'it, which needs more reinforcement, they penalised even one who planted inadvertently (Mishna Terumot 2:3; Gittin 54a; Rambam 1:12).

It is permitted to throw fruit remains in the garden or in the field. And although perhaps a tree will grow from this, since that is not his intention, and it is also not clear that a tree will grow from it, there is no prohibition in it.

notes_en.en:
It is explained in Gittin 53b, regarding one who plants a tree in Shevi'it, who must uproot it, that planting is forbidden by Torah law. And so wrote R. Shimshon and Rash Sirillo. On the other hand, we learned in Mo'ed Katan 3a that only four kinds of work are forbidden by a Torah negative prohibition, and planting is not among them. And so wrote the Rambam 1:4; Rabbeinu Tam; and Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20:4. Thus the prohibition of planting is rabbinic. And one may explain that in Gittin they said that planting is forbidden by Torah law because it involves cancelling the positive Torah mitzva of resting, like ploughing (above note 1), but there is no Torah negative prohibition in it (and so wrote Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan, se'if katan 4). And it seems that this is the view of most poskim, and so it appears from Maran the Rav in Kuntres Aḥaron 6. There is another kind of sowing, by ploughing, that is, one ploughs in order to cover the seeds, and it too is included in the Torah prohibition of sowing (Meiri, Mo'ed Katan 3a; Radbaz; Maran the Rav in Kuntres Aḥaron 6).
It is forbidden rabbinically to plant a tree seedling in a large clod of earth; and although regarding orla its planting is not considered a new planting, nevertheless this planting helps the growth of the tree greatly, and its law is like fertilising and the other kinds of work that improve growth, which are forbidden rabbinically. And some permitted this entirely, and some forbade it by Torah law (see Ketif Shevi'it 1:7, note 9).
When they began to use a sowing machine, some raised the argument that perhaps one who sows by machine does not transgress a Torah prohibition, for he does not sow by hand in the manner of sowing of which the Torah spoke; and perhaps sowing by machine is forbidden as grama (indirect action), and then in a pressing situation one could sow in this way (see Har Tzvi OḤ 1:208). But in practice, sowing by machine is like any sowing, since this is an accepted way of sowing today. And we have already learned (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 9:9) that the essence of grama is that it be done with a complete departure from what is accepted.

sections.body_en:
Included in the mitzva of shemita is not to cut the branches of fruit trees in the way of those who prune, in order to improve the tree and encourage the growth of the fruit, as it is said (Vayikra 25:4): "And you shall not prune your vineyard." This kind of work is named after the branches of the vine, which are called zemorot. And although there are Rishonim from whom one could learn that only with the vine is the work of pruning forbidden by Torah law, whereas with the other trees pruning is forbidden rabbinically, in practice the view of the decisive majority of the Rishonim is that the work of pruning is forbidden by Torah law with all trees. And it is named after the branches of the vine because the benefit of pruning in the vine is very noticeable. But since with the other fruit trees too pruning is very beneficial, with all trees pruning is forbidden by Torah law.

The pruning forbidden by Torah law is cutting the branches in a way that helps the growth of the tree and the fruit, and every farmer and gardener knows what correct and beneficial pruning is. But there are other kinds of cutting branches at a place different from ordinary pruning; and since their aim is different, for example to prevent diseases, to prevent excessive shade or to keep the tree healthy in the long term, and they help less the growth of the tree and the fruit, their prohibition is rabbinic. And we have already learned that all the kinds of work forbidden rabbinically are permitted for sustaining the tree, that is, in order to prevent significant damage for the eighth year. Therefore it is permitted to cut branches in which a disease has spread, so that it will not spread and harm the tree. And likewise it is permitted to cut suckers that grew from the rootstock of the tree (below the graft), which, if they continue to grow, will harm the main tree.5

When the trimming is not for the benefit of the tree but for other reasons, it is permitted to trim the tree, on condition that the trimming be different from the usual way of pruning, so that one will not appear as one who prunes in a forbidden way; for example, instead of pruning part of the branch, he should cut the whole of it. Included in this permission, it is permitted to cut branches that extend over the path and interfere with the passage of passers-by, and likewise it is permitted to trim branches for firewood, or to roof the sukka with them. When there is no one there who knows how to depart from the usual way of pruning, an ordinary person may cut the branches in his own way; for since he does not know how one prunes, it is reasonable that he will not cut in the way that helps improve the tree and the fruit.6 And see halakha 10 regarding forbidden pruning of non-fruit trees.

notes_en.en:
Plainly, the prohibition of pruning includes all trees, and what is said, "And you shall not prune your vineyard", is an example, just as we find in many mitzvot that the Torah gave an example and meant everything similar to it; and in the shemita too it commanded: "the grapes of your untended vine you shall not gather", and it meant all kinds of fruit. And so we learned in Bava Batra 80b, regarding cutting a virgin sycamore, that its pruning is forbidden by Torah law, as all the commentators explained there. Admittedly, the Ḥazon Ish 21:15 learned from R. Shimshon on Shevi'it 2:3 and other Rishonim that pruning other trees is trimming (kirsum), whose prohibition is rabbinic. But the decisive majority of the Rishonim wrote explicitly that pruning all fruit trees is forbidden by Torah law; and so wrote the Rambam 1:2, the Ra'avad, the Semag, the Ḥinukh, the Tosafot Yom Tov. And so wrote the Rashbam, Ramban, Rashba, Ritva, Ran and Meiri on Bava Batra 80b. And so ruled the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20:2; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:2. And Maran Rav Kook in Shabbat Ha-Aretz, and the Or Same'aḥ on the Rambam 1:15, wrote that the prohibition of cutting rice is because there is a Torah prohibition of pruning even with seeds. And what the Ḥazon Ish learned from R. Shimshon is also not compelling, for there are different kinds of cutting branches, such as kirsum, zirud, pisul, kitum and peiruk, and all of these are forbidden rabbinically, since they are not the essential pruning meant for making the tree and the fruit grow and improving them, but are actions different from ordinary pruning and meant to support growth, for example by removing the blossom, or trimmings meant to remove branches that dried up and may bring diseases or that cause much shade, as explained in Mishna Shevi'it 2:3; Bavli Mo'ed Katan 3a; Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 11. And although many books followed the Ḥazon Ish, either because they sought a way to permit pruning, which is very much needed for making the fruit grow, or because they relied on his greatness, in practice one should not rely on his view even in a pressing situation, because it runs against the view of the Rishonim and the Aḥaronim.
And it seems that the definition of the pruning forbidden by Torah law is simple: what farmers and gardeners are accustomed to do in order to make the tree grow in the best way is the pruning forbidden by Torah law; and what is considered a significant departure from this, to the point that it is no longer considered good pruning, is forbidden rabbinically. Accordingly, as long as mechanical pruning in the vineyard was considered significantly less good, its prohibition was rabbinic. But today, because of the time it saves, in many places it has become the ordinary pruning even though it is less precise, and therefore its prohibition is by Torah law.
Maran the Rav wrote (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 11; Mishpat Kohen 67) that the pruning of the vine forbidden by Torah law was at the tips of the branches or parts of them, which encourages growth and the giving of more fruit; whereas the pruning of the branches down to the trunk that is customary today in grafted vines is meant to sustain the vine for many years, and therefore its prohibition is rabbinic. However, it is clear that what is customary today, pruning some of the branches that one wants to give fruit after two or three buds, is the pruning forbidden by Torah law.

It seems difficult: even trimming for another purpose, since it helps improve the tree, involves the prohibition of 'pesik reisha' (an inevitable consequence), whose prohibition is by Torah law. And so is the view of the Tosafot, Sanhedrin 26a, s.v. 'la'akel', that even one who needs [the branches] for the tree may cut only to the extent that the cutting is harmful to the tree. But the Rambam (Commentary on the Mishna 4:6) wrote explicitly that these trimmings are permitted since their intention is not to improve the tree. And it is implied that this is the law even if he cuts at the place suited to pruning. And Maran the Rav (Kuntres Aḥaron 9) learned from this that there is no prohibition of pesik reisha in Shevi'it. Thus far. And so is the law according to the Rambam regarding those who wish to cut trees for firewood or for sekhakh or for hoops. (And perhaps one can learn this from the fact that it is permitted to pick the fruit of the shemita, and picking too causes growth in the next season, like pruning.)
However, according to the Tosafot (who hold that pesik reisha is forbidden in Shevi'it), one must clarify how they permitted rabbinic trimmings for okmei, since while caring for okmei he also improves the tree. And Maran the Rav wrote (Kuntres Aḥaron 11) that although it is a pesik reisha for avruyei, it is permitted. And the Ratzia"h explained (Olelot Shevi'it 2) that since his intention is explicitly for okmei alone, and it is different from the intention of avruyei, the intention of okmei cancels the side benefit of improvement. Thus far. And one must say this, for otherwise every permission for okmei would be cancelled, since every action of okmei improves somewhat (above note 2).

sections.body_en:
Ploughing is one of the important kinds of work in agriculture, and its aim is to split the ground with the teeth of the plough and make furrows in it, in order to sow seeds in them, and in the course of this to uproot the wild grasses so that they will not harm the seeds. In addition, ploughing greatly improves the soil, by making it loose and aerated; the organic materials that nourish the plants are improved, and the roots can spread in it easily and draw their nourishment. And when there are many wild grasses and thorns in the ground, or when the ground has become hard and compacted, one must plough it two or three times before sowing. In the past the plough was drawn by an ox or a horse or a donkey, and today one ploughs with a tractor, and various ploughs have been developed to respond optimally to the various needs. Digging pits for planting seedlings is also included in the work of ploughing.

Ploughing is forbidden in Shevi'it by Torah law. And although we learned that only four kinds of work were forbidden by a Torah negative prohibition, nevertheless there is a positive mitzva to rest from the work of the field in Shevi'it, as it is said (Vayikra 25:4): "But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land"; and anyone who does work regularly in his usual way as in the other years cancels a positive Torah mitzva. And likewise it is said (Shemot 34:21): "In ploughing time and in harvest you shall rest," that is, one must rest from the first agricultural work, which is ploughing, until the last, which is harvest; and in the course of this we learned that ploughing is a great work involving much trouble, and one who engages in it cancels the resting. However, some hold that the work of ploughing is forbidden rabbinically.7

Hoeing, like ploughing, is meant to turn over the ground in order to improve it and to uproot weeds; but ploughing is done with great force by a plough and over the whole area of the field, whereas hoeing is done by hand or with a hoe around the bases of the trees. Therefore ploughing, by which the main work of the ground is done, is forbidden by Torah law, whereas hoeing, which is meant for small needs, is a derivative of ploughing; and since its prohibition is rabbinic, it is permitted to hoe in order to prevent significant damage (Mo'ed Katan 3a; see Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:7, 2).

Therefore, if the roots of the tree became exposed and the tree will dry up if they are not covered, it is permitted to cover them with a hoe. And likewise if the soil is about to dry out and harden and in the course of this sever the roots, it is permitted to hoe it in order to soften it so that it will not harden. But not for the sake of sustaining the tree, hoeing is forbidden. And likewise it is forbidden to crumble clods in the field by hand or foot, for there is benefit in this for the ground and the plants.

notes_en.en: According to the great majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, ploughing is forbidden by Torah law. And so wrote Rashi, Tosafot, R. Shimshon, the Ra'avad, the Rosh, the Ritva, the Ran, the Peri Ḥadash and R. Akiva Eiger. And it is clear that there is a positive prohibition in ploughing, either because it is said regarding Shevi'it (Vayikra 25:4): "But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land," or from what is said regarding Shabbat (Shemot 34:21): "In ploughing time and in harvest you shall rest"; and Rabbi Akiva learned that this instruction was said regarding Shevi'it, that even on the eve of Shevi'it it is forbidden to plough, and even after Shevi'it it is forbidden to reap the grain of Shevi'it (Mishna Shevi'it 1:4; Rosh Ha-Shana 9a; and according to Rabbi Yishmael this verse deals with Shabbat, but he too can agree that one can learn from it that ploughing cancels the mitzva of resting with which we were commanded in the Torah). And the Talmud is divided over whether ploughing also involves a negative prohibition for which one receives lashes (Yerushalmi Kilayim 8:1; Bavli Mo'ed Katan 3a). And regarding the words of the Rambam there is doubt: on the one hand he mentioned the verse "In ploughing time and in harvest you shall rest" (Rambam 1:1), from which we learned that the prohibition of ploughing is by Torah law; on the other hand he wrote about one who ploughs that he receives rabbinic lashes of rebellion (there 4), and from this the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20:1 learned that ploughing is forbidden rabbinically. And Maran Rav Kook (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 2) explained that regular ploughing, in the way of all the years, is forbidden by a positive prohibition. And some hold that the view of the Rambam is that ploughing to improve the soil around the trees so that they will grow more is forbidden by Torah law, and ploughing to improve the soil in a place where there are not yet trees and seeds is forbidden rabbinically (Radbaz).

sections.body_en:
It is permitted to dig pits and trenches for building, since only ploughing or digging for the work of the field was forbidden (Sifra Behar 1:4). But one must be careful not to level afterwards the earth taken out of the digging; rather, it should be piled in a heap. And on paths, where people walk, it is permitted to level the ground, for it is clear that levelling the ground there is not for an agricultural purpose.

It is forbidden rabbinically to clear stones from the field, whether large stones or small stones, whether from one's own field or from one's fellow's field. And likewise it is forbidden to level the ground and fill holes with earth, since these actions prepare the ground for sowing and planting (Rambam 2:10-11).

When a person needs stones for building a house or a wall, he may take stones lying in his field on top of other stones and rocks, but not stones lying on the ground. For if he takes those lying on the ground, he appears to be preparing his field for sowing. And if these are stones that are evidently being taken for building, he may take them even if they touch the ground. And if he is a contractor engaged in building, since it is known that his main intention is to take them for building, he may take even stones that are not evidently for building. And likewise a person may take stones from an ownerless field or from his fellow's field for building; for since it is not his field, everyone knows that he is taking the stones for building and not for the sake of the field (Rambam 2:8; 10; 12. And see below 11 regarding ornamental gardens).8

A building contractor who must prepare the ground around the buildings for a garden, and as long as he does not do so he cannot hand over the apartments to the buyers, and he would suffer a very great loss from this, may hire a non-Jew to level the ground and spread garden soil over it so that he can hand over the apartments to the buyers. For the halakha is that in a pressing situation it is permitted to tell a non-Jew to do work whose prohibition is rabbinic, like the law of 'shevut de-shevut' (below 5:10; and see Be-Ohalah Shel Torah 3:20).

It is permitted to lay irrigation pipes in the garden soil for watering the field; for since watering the field is permitted, it is also permitted to prepare the means of watering for watering in the shemita year or in the year after it, on condition that he does not afterwards level the ground, because of the prohibition of ploughing. And if the digging looks like ploughing for sowing or planting, he should place the water pipes beside the digging, so that it will be evident that it is for watering (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:9; Mishpetei Eretz 6:11-12).

notes_en.en: These laws are detailed in the Mishna (3:5-10), and I have written the rules relevant to us, as emerges from the Rambam 2:6-14. In summary: a person may take stones from his field for building even though he also intends to prepare his field for sowing, on condition that he does not appear as one who does this to prepare the field. So it emerges from the Rambam 2:7-8. Therefore, if he began to take the stones of a wall before Shevi'it, he may take all of them. And likewise, when he does not intend to prepare his field for sowing, he may take all the stones of the wall; but if he also wants to prepare his field for sowing or planting, he must leave the row of the wall close to the ground, unless it is evident from the stones of the wall that they are very suitable for building. And when he takes ordinary stones from the field for building, he should not take those touching the ground, for he appears to be preparing his field; but from his fellow's field he may take even those touching the ground.

sections.title_en: 8. Work on the Tree and Its Preservation
sections.body_en:
Let us repeat the rule of the kinds of work: sowing, pruning and ploughing are forbidden by Torah law, and therefore it is forbidden to do them in every situation. But all the other kinds of work that prepare the ground and help the growth of trees and field crops are forbidden rabbinically. If they prepare the ground, they are derivatives of the work of ploughing, and if they help growth, they are derivatives of the work of sowing and pruning. And although their prohibition is rabbinic, one who does them regularly as in all the years, in order to improve his field and his trees, cancels a positive Torah mitzva, which commanded resting in Shevi'it (above 1). And when there is a need to do them in order to prevent damage, even if one must take much trouble over them, there is no prohibition in them. And from here we will continue to the details of the halakha:

It is forbidden rabbinically to pull out weeds or to cut them with a sickle or to spray them with pesticides, for there is benefit in this for the field and the trees. But when the weeds cause significant damage to the trees or the ornamental plants, it is permitted to remove them. And likewise it is permitted to remove them in a place where there is a concern that snakes and scorpions will find shelter in them, or that a fire will spread through them. Wherever possible, the harmful weeds should be removed by cutting or spraying and not by hoeing or pulling out the weeds, which improve the ground more; but for lack of choice this too is permitted.9

It is forbidden to support young trees with a stake so that they will grow straight upwards or so that their branches will spread out to the sides. But if the support is necessary to prevent damage to them, it is permitted (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:5, 13).

When fruit trees are planted densely, it is forbidden to uproot some of them so that they will not harm one another's growth. And although there is no Torah prohibition of pruning in this, since one does not cut the branches of the tree whose growth one wants to encourage, rabbinically it is forbidden. And when his intention is to uproot the trees for firewood, although he also benefits from thinning the trees, he may cut the trees. And this is on condition that he uproots one or two trees in a row; but if he needed to uproot three trees, he should cut them close to the ground and not take them out by the root, so that he will not appear as one preparing his field for sowing or planting (Mishna Shevi'it 4:4; Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:18). And if the superfluous trees are actually harmful, to the point that if they are not uprooted in Shevi'it significant damage will be caused to the remaining trees that will continue into the eighth year, it is permitted to uproot the superfluous ones even when he does not intend to use the trees for firewood.

notes_en.en: Some are stringent and forbid spraying weeds, because they have the holiness of Shevi'it since they are fit for animal food, and consequently it is forbidden to destroy them. But we find in the Mishna 8:1, regarding a plant fit for various uses, that a person's intention is what determines whether it will be considered human food, animal food or wood, which has no holiness of Shevi'it. Thus even a plant fit for animal food, if in practice people are not accustomed to feed animals with it, has no holiness of Shevi'it. And so it is customary to rule (see Mishpetei Eretz 4, note 24; Be-Ohalah Shel Torah 3:27). Therefore it is permitted to spray and kill weeds. And one who wishes to be stringent should use germination inhibitors from the outset.

sections.body_en:
Some say that the law of watering is like the other kinds of work forbidden rabbinically, which were permitted for sustaining and forbidden for improving. Therefore it is permitted in Shevi'it to water trees and bushes that are usually watered in all the years, in order to save them from death or from significant damage that would continue into the eighth year. But it is forbidden to water them so that they will be beautiful and give fruit as they usually gave in the other years (Rambam). And some say that the law of watering is more lenient than the other kinds of work, because there is a constant need for it and no expertise is needed to do it, and also usually it involves no great trouble; therefore it was permitted even for improving the tree. Moreover, since it is hard to distinguish the amount of watering required to prevent damage, the Sages did not make distinctions in the matter and permitted watering as in the other years. In practice, one should take a middle way: for improving the tree it is forbidden to water, but when it is permitted to water in order to prevent damage, it is permitted to water in an ordinary amount. And especially today, when watering is done by opening a tap and there is no trouble in adding water.10

It is permitted to spray in order to prevent various diseases in the trees, because diseases in the tree or in the leaves may cause significant damage that would continue into the eighth year. And likewise it is permitted to spray against insects that may harm the tree. But it is forbidden to spray in order to feed the tree with hormones that encourage the growth of the tree and the fruit. And likewise it is forbidden to spray against insects that damage the fruit. It is permitted to spray the ground with germination inhibitors or herbicides, so that weeds will not grow in it and take away its strength, because without this spraying significant damage may be caused for the eighth year.

It is forbidden to give manure and fertiliser to the trees, because usually fertilising is not meant to sustain the trees but to improve their growth. And one who wants his trees to continue to develop in Shevi'it should give them a double portion of fertiliser before Shevi'it begins, and they will be nourished from it during the year. However, if it became clear through reliable testing that there is an urgent need for fertilising in order to sustain the trees, it is permitted to fertilise them so that they will not die or be significantly damaged.

The Sages forbade taking manure out of the cowsheds to the field, even when the intention is to keep it there until the next year, because he appears as one fertilising his field. But it is permitted to remove the manure to a place unfit for sowing. And one who wants to remove the manure to the field should wait until after the season in which one is accustomed to fertilise the field, and pile the manure in heaps of at least one hundred and fifty se'ah (about 1,080 litres), or place the manure in a heap on a rock or on a sheet of metal or plastic (Rambam 2:1-3).11

notes_en.en: Plainly, the law of watering is like the law of the other rabbinic kinds of work, which were permitted only for sustaining the tree so that it will not die or be damaged; and so it is implied from Mo'ed Katan 2b, where they discussed watering as they discuss the other kinds of work. And so it emerges from the words of the Rambam 1:10. And so wrote the Ria"z and the Tiferet Yisrael. By contrast, some were more lenient about watering, because it is an unimportant kind of work since it is done constantly (Nimukei Yosef), and it is not work of the ground (Rivav), and it is hard to distinguish between a great and a small loss (Mabit 2:64; Ḥut Ha-Shani 1:10). And in Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:8, regarding a rain-fed field, he wrote both views, with an inclination to the lenient view. However, he wrote that one should not water in order to produce fruit (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:15, 4). In practice, in a time of need one may rely on the lenient views, for watering is rabbinic and Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic. In any case, as a general ruling it is right to follow the middle way, and so it is accepted to rule.

The Sages penalised one who ploughed or fertilised his field in Shevi'it, that he may not sow it in the eighth year, nor may his field be leased from him in the eighth year. And if he died, his son may sow it in the eighth year (Mishna Shevi'it 4:2; Rambam 1:13). And Maran Rav Kook wrote that this penalty applies at a time when most of the public are careful about this, and therefore they penalised one who broke the fence and brazenly ploughed or fertilised his field in Shevi'it. But when many stumble in this, since they do not do so brazenly, the Sages did not penalise them (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:13).

sections.body_en:
One who works on non-fruit trees in the way he works in the other years, since he is not resting, cancels a positive Torah mitzva. However, as regards the negative prohibitions, the prohibition of planting non-fruit trees and non-fruit plants, and likewise of pruning them and tending them, is rabbinic (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:5; see below 3:6).

In a pressing situation it is permitted to plant non-fruit trees through non-Jews, since the prohibition of telling a non-Jew to do work is also rabbinic, and this is like the law of 'shevut de-shevut' on Shabbat, which is permitted in a pressing situation. Therefore, in the past, when people suffered from malaria, and the doctors held that planting eucalyptus trees could help dry the swamps, purify the air and prevent the spread of the disease, it was permitted to tell a non-Jew to plant them in Shevi'it.

And likewise, when a main road must be paved, there is a need to do landscaping work at the sides of the road, for purifying the air, preventing erosion and for beauty. And if the road is opened to traffic and the landscaping work is postponed until after Shevi'it, great damage will be caused to the contractor; and there is also a concern that meanwhile the earth will be washed onto the road, and during the landscaping work a certain risk will arise to the lives of the drivers and the workers. And if the opening of the road is postponed, the safety risks of the old road will continue, and the public will continue to suffer from traffic congestion. Therefore, if they did not manage to arrange the landscaping work before Shevi'it, it is permitted to have it done by non-Jews in Shevi'it.12

notes_en.en: In the Yerushalmi (Shevi'it 4:4) it is explained that according to the first Tanna it is forbidden to burn the reeds of a bush in order to thicken its trunk, and according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel it is permitted; and likewise according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel it is permitted to plant a non-fruit tree. And the Rambam 1:5 ruled that it is forbidden to plant a non-fruit tree in Shevi'it. And although some hold that according to some of the Rishonim the prohibition is by Torah law (Ḥazon Ish, and so it is implied from Rash Sirillo), we have already learned (in halakha 4) that even regarding a fruit tree, according to the Rambam and those who agree with him, the prohibition is rabbinic, and the Mahari"t Tzahalon explained that this is because planting does not produce fruit in the shemita. All the more so with a non-fruit tree, which never gives fruit. And so the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 19:5 wrote that the prohibition is rabbinic. And the prohibition of planting a non-fruit tree is not only for the sake of wood but also for beauty and a fence (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:5). In any case, it seems that one who works on non-fruit trees as in all the years cancels a positive Torah mitzva, as explained in halakha 1 and note 1. However, it seems that one who plants because of a pressing situation does not transgress the positive mitzva, for he is considered as planting occasionally, since he planted only because of the pressure. And when it concerns a very great loss, and perhaps even a remote concern for life, as in the case of paving a main road, one may be lenient even through a Jew, like the law of shevut de-shevut for a great need and a mitzva; for Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, and likewise planting non-fruit trees is rabbinic. But in practice, since one can make use of a non-Jew, one should be lenient in this only through a non-Jew, for by this another 'shevut' is added, as explained below 5:9. Similarly the Maharil Diskin (27:24) wrote regarding planting eucalyptus trees through a non-Jew for the sake of health. And in Responsa Netzer Mata'ai 28 he permitted Jews to plant non-fruit trees in the forests of the Jewish National Fund, in order to hold lands against Arab trespassers and so that they would have a livelihood after their immigration to the Land. And this is because in his view the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, that there is no prohibition of planting non-fruit trees, and even the first Tanna does not disagree with him. And it seems that he could have argued that in a pressing situation one must rule like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel against the first Tanna, but there is no room to say that the first Tanna agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. In any case, according to our reality today, in all pressing situations one may be lenient only through a non-Jew.

sections.body_en:
Just as it is permitted to do kinds of work forbidden rabbinically for sustaining fruit trees, so that they will not die or wither, so it is permitted to do these kinds of work for sustaining trees and bushes in ornamental gardens. For the aim of the shemita is not to harm the trees and bushes and to require the owners of gardens to set them up anew after every shemita; rather the mitzva is that we rest from work meant to improve them. And one should not argue that since they do not produce fruit there will be no loss if they die in the shemita; for it is a fact that people invest time and money to sustain them, so if they die or wither a loss will be caused. And since all the kinds of work the Sages forbade are forbidden only for improving the plants, it is permitted to do them in order to prevent significant damage to the ornamental plants that would continue into the eighth year and require great expense to restore.

Therefore all the rules stated regarding fruit trees apply to ornamental plants. It is permitted to spray the plants to save them from diseases and pests, but it is forbidden to spray them with hormones that encourage growth. It is forbidden to fertilise ornamental plants; only if it became clear after testing that without fertilising the plant will be significantly damaged is it permitted to fertilise it (above 9). It is forbidden to hoe around the plants; but if the roots became exposed or may be torn, it is permitted to hoe around them in order to prevent significant damage to the plants (above 6).

It is forbidden to pull out weeds or to cut them with a sickle or to spray them with pesticides, for there is benefit in this for the field and the trees. But it is permitted when the weeds may kill the ornamental plants or cause them significant damage. When the danger is known in advance, it is preferable to use spraying that prevents germination. And if the weeds have already grown, they should be cut above the surface of the ground, or killed by spraying, but not uprooted, for uprooting turns over the ground and improves it like ploughing. Only when there is no possibility at all of removing them by cutting or spraying is it permitted to uproot them in order to prevent significant damage to the ornamental plants (above 8).

It is permitted to water ornamental plants in order to prevent damage to them, and when watering them, it is permitted to water them in an ordinary amount (above 9).

It is forbidden to improve the ground by clearing stones, filling holes or hoeing. But it is permitted to remove by hand stones and refuse that make the garden unsightly, for it is evident that the intention is not to improve the ground but only to beautify the appearance of the garden (Sefer Ha-Shemita 5:4).

One who is accustomed to neglect his garden may not do in the shemita kinds of work for sustaining the plants beyond what he is accustomed to do in all the years. This is because the permission is in order to prevent loss, and since he is accustomed not to be concerned about this loss in all the years, it is implied that it is not a loss for him.

sections.title_en: 12. Trimming, Mowing the Lawn and Preparing the Garden for Shemita
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to trim the branches of plants, because trimming encourages new growth; but in order to prevent damage it is permitted. Therefore it is permitted to trim diseased branches, or suckers that came out of the rootstock and may take over the tree. And likewise it is permitted to trim branches that have spread onto the path and interfere with passage. And likewise it is permitted to trim branches for sekhakh or for firewood. And if the one trimming is a professional gardener, he must depart from the usual way of trimming, so that it will be evident that he is not trimming in order to encourage growth. And if he is not a professional, he may trim in his own way (above 5).

And likewise it is forbidden to trim the branches of flowering bushes, or flowers that have grown, in order to encourage the growth of more branches and flowers. But it is permitted to pick flowers to decorate the house, even though incidentally this encourages further growth. And the same law applies to rose bushes: it is permitted to pick roses to put them in a vase, and one who knows that it is customary to cut them in the middle of the stem should cut lower or higher. But it is forbidden to cut the flowers or the bulbs in order to encourage another wave of flowering.

In many gardens bushes are planted to serve as a hedge shaped like a wall, and then the question arises whether it is permitted to trim these bushes in order to keep their shape. In practice the law depends on the state of the hedge. If the bush has already formed a dense wall, since there is no further benefit in its continuing to grow, and from the gardener's standpoint it would be preferable that it not grow more, it is permitted to trim it in order to keep its fine shape, for this is not trimming for growth but a haircut for beauty. But as long as the bush does not fill all the space allotted to it, it is forbidden to trim it, because trimming helps it continue to grow so that it will form a dense and full wall (Ketif Shevi'it 49:23-24).

Similarly regarding a lawn. If the lawn has already completely covered the surface of the ground with full grass, there is no further need for it to continue to grow, and the whole aim of mowing is only to keep its fine appearance, and this is permitted. And likewise it is permitted to cut the runners of the grass that spread beyond the area allotted to it. But if the lawn has not yet completely filled the whole surface of the ground, there is benefit in mowing the lawn to encourage its continued growth, and consequently it is forbidden to mow it in Shevi'it (Ketif Shevi'it 50:13-14; and see Mishpetei Eretz 4:19, 23).

From the experience of veteran gardeners, when the garden is prepared well before the shemita, the garden will look fine throughout the whole year. Admittedly, one will not be able to plant seasonal flowers in it, nor will one be able to have repeated waves of flowering, but the garden will look green, fine and respectable. For this one must be careful to trim well from the beginning of the sixth year, and to fertilise the ground with compost or slow-release fertilisers. Likewise one must be careful to keep the garden clean of weeds, and to spray the ground with germination-inhibiting substances. And instead of seasonal flowers it is recommended to plant biennial flowers in the sixth year (in the book 'Ketif Shevi'it' there is detailed guidance for professional gardeners and garden owners on how to act before the shemita and during the shemita).

Any work that can be done before the shemita, even though it is meant for sustaining and saving from loss, must be done before the shemita. For the mitzva is to rest in the shemita, and only for lack of choice, in order to prevent loss, is it permitted to do work. And one who could have done work before the shemita and postponed it to the shemita must ask a Torah scholar whether he may do it in the shemita (above halakha 3).

sections.title_en: 13. A House, a Greenhouse and an Unperforated Pot
sections.body_en:
The Sages were in doubt whether the laws of Shevi'it apply inside a house. The reference is to houses whose floor is earth, as was common until a few generations ago, in which it was possible to plant bushes and sow seeds. The question is whether the mitzva of Shevi'it applies to the whole land, including the place inside the house, as it is said (Vayikra 25:2): "Then shall the land keep a Sabbath to the Lord." Or whether the mitzva applies specifically in the field, that is, under the open sky, as it is said (ibid. 4): "You shall not sow your field," and consequently the prohibitions of Shevi'it do not apply inside the house (Yerushalmi Orla 1:2).

But if they placed pots without a hole inside the house, the law of Shevi'it does not apply to them. For in addition to growing in a house and not in a field, they are also detached from the land, and so they are completely separated from the place to which the laws of shemita apply.

Some say that the same law applies to pots grown in greenhouses: if they have no hole, the laws of Shevi'it do not apply to them, because it makes no difference what the house is made of, stones, wood or plastic sheets. But it seems more correct to follow the view of those who hold that the law of a greenhouse is like a field and not like a house, since the greenhouse is meant for growing vegetables and the house is not. Even so, since the basis of the law of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, and growing in an unperforated pot is also rabbinic, in a pressing situation those who wish to be lenient may grow vegetables in greenhouses on a detached growing medium.

The greenhouse must be at least ten tefachim high (76 cm) and at least 4 amot wide (about 182 cm). And according to many, for the greenhouse to be defined as a house it must have a majority of walls.

In practice, those who grow vegetables in greenhouses in Shevi'it are accustomed to plant in pots that have a hole, in order to drain the excess water from them; and so that they will be considered to have the law of an unperforated pot, they place the perforated pots on a thick plastic sheet through which no root can penetrate, and by this they are detached from the ground and considered unperforated pots.13

notes_en.en:
The doubt regarding a house is brought in the Yerushalmi Orla 1:2. Some say that since Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, the doubt is resolved leniently. And so wrote the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan 20, se'if katan 52; and Rav Herzog. On the other hand some hold that when the basis of the mitzva is from the Torah, even though its law in practice is rabbinic, it is considered a doubt in a Torah law, to be resolved stringently (Ḥazon Ish 22:1). And some say that the whole doubt is whether there is a Torah prohibition inside a house, but a rabbinic prohibition there certainly is (see Minḥat Shlomo 51:7). And Maran Rav Kook raised reasons on both sides and decided that only in a case of loss may one be lenient, and one should treat the fruit as having holiness out of doubt (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 1:3; Kuntres Aḥaron 3). And some are stringent and hold that the law of a greenhouse is like a field and not like a house, for an ordinary house is liable to harm growth whereas a greenhouse helps it (Rav Elyashiv, Rav Nissim Karelitz). And so it seems plainly. And those who are lenient argue that the main reason for the exemption is that a house is not considered a field and was excluded from the mitzva (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Rav Wosner). And some answer that the greenhouse only protects the plants, but as regards growth it is often more harmful than helpful (Mishpetei Eretz 7:5; Ketif Shevi'it 17, 8). In practice, Rav Yisraeli permitted only where there are two rabbinic factors, such as rabbinic kinds of work through a non-Jew, or planting a non-fruit tree in a root ball. And Rav Eliyahu permitted even with one rabbinic factor (see Ketif Shevi'it 17:1). And as we have learned, those who wish to be lenient with detached growing media may, in a time of need, be lenient even with kinds of work whose basis is from the Torah, since Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic. Maran Rav Kook further wrote (Kuntres Aḥaron 3) that perhaps the house must be built before the planting or sowing, and perhaps it must be four amot wide. Thus far his words. And with a net roof, its density must be more than 50% shade (Rav Eliyahu). Some say that walls are not needed and the roof alone makes the place a house (Har Tzvi Zera'im 2:34). And some say that a majority of walls ten tefachim high is needed (Rav Shapira). And see Ketif Shevi'it 17:3-4.
The law of a pot: in many halakhot we have learned that the law of a perforated pot placed above the ground is like the law of the ground, because through the hole in it, it is considered attached to the earth. Therefore there is an obligation from the Torah to separate terumot and ma'asrot from what grows in it. But if it has no hole, it is considered detached from the land, and only rabbinically does one separate terumot and ma'asrot from it (Mishna Demai 5:10). And likewise regarding one who reaps on Shabbat: in a perforated pot the prohibition is from the Torah, and in an unperforated one it is rabbinic (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 336:7; Mishna Berura 42). And so too regarding Shevi'it: if there is a hole in a pot placed above the ground, all the Torah prohibitions apply to it; and if there is no hole in it, its law is like something detached from the ground, and only rabbinically do the prohibitions of Shevi'it apply to it (Neḥpa Ba-Kesef, Yoreh De'ah 5). Consequently in any case of doubt one should be lenient with it. And as we have learned, the law of Shevi'it in a house is in doubt; if so, with an unperforated pot the halakha is to be lenient. This is in addition to the fact that the very law of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic. In practice, the Ḥazon Ish 22:1; 26:4 wrote that one who is lenient with an unperforated pot inside a house even in Torah kinds of work has something to rely on. And Rav Yisraeli, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Rav Elyashiv, Rav Eliyahu and Yalkut Yosef pp. 210-222 were lenient in this from the outset. And those who are meticulous also sell the pots to a non-Jew (and see Ketif Shevi'it 18, 36). The pot must be of a size that can be moved; according to Rav Eliyahu, one person must be able to lift it, and according to Rav Yisraeli, anything less than forty se'ah has the law of a pot (Ketif Shevi'it 18, 22). Forty se'ah are 288 litres (by the precise calculation according to the Rambam). A hole the size of a small root is about one millimetre in diameter (though regarding the years of orla, for it to be considered attached to the ground, the stringent practice is to require a diameter of 2.5 cm). And see Ketif Shevi'it chapter 18 for all the details of the laws.
Water-grown crops (hydroponics), that is, plants grown in water enriched with chemical fertilisers: some are stringent (see Har Tzvi 31; Maharil Diskin 27:1). And some are lenient, since this is not the way of growing in soil (Neḥpa Ba-Kesef, Yoreh De'ah 5; Ma'amar Mordechai 4:9). And inside a greenhouse it is obvious that one may be lenient. And see below 3, note 8, on the law of mushrooms.

sections.title_en: 14. Pots in the Garden and in the House
sections.body_en:
Garden soil placed above a house or above a car park, even though the soil rests on concrete that separates it from the ground of the world, has the law of soil in the ground, and all the laws of Shevi'it apply to it. This is because the concrete itself is completely attached to the ground of the world and the soil rests on it permanently, so that the soil is considered part of the ground of the world. And likewise a planter permanently attached to the wall of the house is considered attached to the ground of the world, and even when it has no hole, the law of the seedlings in it is like the law of seedlings in the garden.

A pot placed in the garden or on an uncovered balcony, whether it has a hole or has no hole, the laws of Shevi'it apply to it. However, if it has a hole in its bottom or in its side opposite its roots the size of a small root, it is considered attached to the earth and the laws of Shevi'it apply to it by Torah law. And if it has no hole the size of a small root, the laws of Shevi'it apply to it rabbinically.

But a pot placed inside the house or on a balcony that has a roof, the laws of Shevi'it do not apply to it, since it is detached from the land and has a roof over it (as explained in the previous halakha). It is permitted to sow and plant in it, and it is also permitted to prune what grows in it. And even if the pot has a hole and is on the ground floor, since it rests on a floor through which no root can pass, it is considered detached from the ground. All this is on condition that the pot can be moved; but if it is fixed in the floor, or so heavy that it cannot be lifted, even if it has no hole it is considered attached to the ground, and the law of the seedlings in it is like those planted in the ground. However, since it is inside a house, as we have learned (in the previous halakha) there is a doubt whether the laws of Shevi'it apply to it, and in a case of loss one may be lenient.14

notes_en.en: The Rosh (Kelal 2:4) wrote that a garden above a roof has the law of a field as regards the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot and orla; and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 294:26; Magen Avraham, Oraḥ Ḥayim 336:14. According to this, one should also be stringent with attached planters (and so wrote Ma'amar Mordechai 9:9, Mishpetei Eretz 8, 25). But what is inside the house is exempt from the laws of Shevi'it, since it is in a house and is considered an unperforated pot. However, according to Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 1, 41:2), the floor tiles on the ground floor do not help for perforated pots. And some are stringent regarding tiles even on higher floors (see Shevet Ha-Levi 6:167, Mishpetei Eretz 8, 6). However, the main halakha is that all kinds of tiles and concrete usually used in houses form a barrier, for no root passes through them. And so wrote the Brit Olam, Kotzer 15, and Yalkut Yosef 4:26.

sections.body_en:
It is permitted to bring a perforated pot from the garden into the house. But one should not take a perforated pot out of the house or from a tiled balcony to the garden, because of the prohibition of planting, since placing it on the earth is considered planting it in the land. And if he places a plastic plate under it, it is considered an unperforated pot and it is permitted.

A pot that broke, if a clod of earth with the roots of the plant still remains, it is permitted to put it again into a similar pot, in order to sustain the plant so that it will not die. But if the clod was in an unperforated pot, it is forbidden to put it into a perforated pot, for by this one improves its status as more planted in the land.

It is permitted to place flower branches and branches of fragrant plants in a vase of water in the courtyard; and although by placing them in water the flowers will bloom and the branches will continue to grow a little, there is no prohibition of sowing in this, since he does not intend to root them.

It is permitted to take a perforated pot out of the house to the courtyard temporarily, not for the purpose of planting it in the courtyard. For example, one who needs to move perforated pots from apartment to apartment may pass through a courtyard and even place them there for a short while. And likewise one who needs to clear the pots out of the house in order to clean it may place them for a short while in the courtyard. Some are stringent to place a barrier between them and the ground, and when moving house to wrap them in nylon (Ma'amar Mordechai 9:8). And one who wishes to be lenient may.15

notes_en.en:
When taking a perforated pot out of the house to the courtyard, one should place a plastic or glass bowl under it. And if the foliage of the plant extends beyond the edge of the pot, the barrier must also be between its foliage and the ground, because even when its branches or leaves are above the ground, it is considered attached to the earth (Mishna Uktzin 2:9; Gittin 22a, Tosafot s.v. 'Batar', and most of the Rishonim). And some are lenient in this, for only regarding impurity is the foliage taken into account (Rambam in the Commentary on the Mishna, there). And it is right to be stringent when placing the pot on the earth.
A perforated pot that rests on pegs is considered as resting on the ground, for the air between them does not form a barrier. And regarding Shabbat it was ruled that one should not lift a perforated pot from the ground onto pegs, for he distances it from the source of its life, and there is an aspect of reaping in this; and likewise one should not bring it near from the pegs to the ground, for he brings it near to the source of its life, and there is an aspect of sowing in this (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 336:8). Regarding shemita, whose law is more lenient, one should not do so permanently, but for a short while in order to move it from house to house it is permitted, for he does not intend to attach it to the ground. And this is the law when he takes the perforated pot out to the courtyard for the sake of cleaning the house. And it also seems that it is permitted to move a perforated pot from place to place in the courtyard, and so ruled Rav Yisraeli and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (see Mishpetei Eretz 8:9). And according to Ma'amar Mordechai 9:8 and Rav Elyashiv one should be stringent. And since the whole law is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient.

sections.body_en:
The shemita year begins on the first of Tishrei. However, it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that already in the thirty days before the seventh year it is forbidden to do kinds of work for the sake of the produce of the field and the trees in Shevi'it. But for young plantings it is permitted to plough until Rosh Ha-Shana, for they need it, and if not, their growth will be damaged. The prohibition of the addition to Shevi'it includes only the important kinds of work mentioned in the Torah that help the growth of the fruit in Shevi'it, and they are: ploughing, pruning and sowing. But kinds of work forbidden rabbinically, such as fertilising and trimming, it is permitted to do until the end of the month of Elul. And although the prohibition of the addition to Shevi'it is thirty days, the Sages added and forbade ploughing a grain field from Pesaḥ onwards, and an orchard from Shavu'ot, because the main purpose of such ploughing is for the coming year.

And all these laws are binding only at a time when they performed the mitzva of the water libation on the altar on the festival of Sukkot, for it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai that the law of the water libation and the addition to Shevi'it are bound up with one another. And indeed, after the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Gamliel and his court took a vote and abolished the laws of the addition to Shevi'it (Mo'ed Katan 3b; 4a; Rambam 3:1; 9).16

notes_en.en:
According to Rabbi Akiva the prohibition of the addition to Shevi'it is from the Torah, as it is said (Shemot 34:21): "In ploughing time and in harvest you shall rest." And according to Rabbi Yishmael it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai. And Rav Ashi explained that the ruling of Rabban Gamliel, who abolished the law of the addition to Shevi'it after the destruction of the Temple, follows the view of Rabbi Yishmael (Mo'ed Katan 3b; 4a; Tosafot s.v. 'Ela'), and so ruled the Rambam 3:1. And the prohibition of the addition to Shevi'it as a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai applies to kinds of work that help the growth of the tree and the fruit in Shevi'it; therefore it is forbidden to plough and prune, but it is obvious that it is permitted to reap and harvest the fruit of the sixth year, for even in Shevi'it this is permitted (Shabbat Ha-Aretz 3:1). And it seems obvious that it was also forbidden to sow in the addition to Shevi'it, since through the sowing the crop will grow in Shevi'it. And the prohibition of the addition to Shevi'it applies to the Torah prohibitions, but rabbinic kinds of work that help growth in Shevi'it, such as fertilising and clearing stones, are permitted in the addition to Shevi'it (Rash, Rosh, Ra'av, on Shevi'it 2:2; Shabbat Ha-Aretz 3:9).
Some say that although the law of the thirty-day addition has been abolished, the addition of a few moments that one is commanded to add on all Shabbatot and festivals, one is commanded to add also before Shevi'it (Tosafot Mo'ed Katan 4a, s.v. 'Mah'). And the addition of the festival of Rosh Ha-Shana also serves for the shemita. And those who wish to be meticulous should say so explicitly (Ma'amar Mordechai 1:13).

sections.title_en: 17. Until When It Is Permitted to Plant and Sow in Our Time
sections.body_en:
Although the law of the addition to Shevi'it has been abolished, it is forbidden to plant bare-root fruit trees after the fifteenth of Av before the shemita, because of how it appears. For one who plants after that is considered, as regards the laws of orla, as though he planted in Shevi'it; for the rule is that thirty days in a year count as a year, and another fourteen days are needed for the roots of the tree to take hold in the earth. It follows that if he planted the tree by the fifteenth of Av, after the tree has had time to take hold, another thirty days of the sixth year will pass over it, and consequently the sixth year will count as the first year in the count of orla. But if he plants the tree from the sixteenth of Av onwards, its first year will be the seventh year, and it will look as though he planted the tree in violation of Shevi'it.

But if the seedling was in a pot that has a hole and was placed on the earth for at least thirty days, then from the time of its planting in the pot the years of orla are already counted for it; and since its roots are in a clod it does not need 14 days to take hold in the earth, and consequently it is permitted to plant it in the earth even on the last day of the sixth year.

Ornamental trees and flower seeds may be planted until close to the beginning of the seventh year, since the law of orla does not apply to them, and also there is no law of the addition to Shevi'it in our time (Rambam, Ramban and the Gra). And although this is the halakha, from the outset it is good to take into account the view of those who are stringent and require that the roots take hold in the earth before the shemita begins (Rabbeinu Tam). That is, a bare-root tree or bush should be planted by the end of the fifteenth of Elul, and seeds until three days before Rosh Ha-Shana. And seedlings in a clod may, even according to the stringent view, be planted until the beginning of Shevi'it, since they do not need time to take root.17

It is important to mention that one is obliged to prepare the orchards and gardens well before the shemita: to carry out deep trimming in the sixth year and to apply slow-release fertilisers, in order to avoid as far as possible in Shevi'it the kinds of work needed to sustain the trees. It is also important to mention that those who want to plant a lawn must plant it at least half a year before the shemita, so that it will have time to take hold and fill the whole area completely (as explained in halakha 12). And those who want to lay turf must lay it about a month before the shemita, in order to ensure that it is fully rooted before the shemita. For if the lawn does not fill the whole area, it will be forbidden to mow it in the shemita, and its watering too will have to be limited to the amount needed so that it will not die, while further watering will be forbidden because it improves its continued growth.

notes_en.en:
According to the Rambam 3:11; the Ramban, Ritva and Meiri on Rosh Ha-Shana 9b; the Gra and Rabbi Akiva Eiger, the prohibition of planting before Shevi'it is because of onlookers who will think he planted in Shevi'it (Gittin 53b), but there is no prohibition against the roots of the planting taking root in the seventh year; therefore it is permitted to plant non-fruit trees on the twenty-ninth of Elul. However, with fruit trees, when the seedling was in a perforated pot with no barrier between it and the earth for thirty days (it is accepted to be stringent and require a hole 2.5 cm in diameter), the years of orla are counted from when it was planted in the pot, and consequently it is permitted to move it from the pot to the earth on the twenty-ninth of Elul. And if it was in an unperforated pot, it is permitted to plant it until the end of the twenty-ninth of Av; for since it is in a clod it does not need time to take hold in the earth, but it needs thirty days so that the sixth year will count as its first year in the count of orla.
