But regarding planting non-fruit trees and seeds there is no restriction at all, since there is no count of orla for them.
And according to Rabbeinu Tam (Tosafot Rosh Ha-Shana 10b, s.v. 'Sheloshim'), the prohibition is that the rooting take place in Shevi'it; in his view there is no difference between fruit trees and non-fruit trees, and the prohibition is from the sixteenth of Elul, for fourteen days is the time it takes trees to take root. And regarding seeds, some say the time for them to take hold is three days (Terumat Ha-Deshen, Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 293:2), and some say fourteen days (Dagul Me-Revava, Rabbi Akiva Eiger); and those who wish to satisfy all views should plant seeds until the fifteenth of Elul (Ma'amar Mordechai 1:8). But I did not write this view above, since in any case the view of most of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is like the Rambam, that there is no restriction at all for seeds and non-fruit trees. It is permitted to sow until the eve of Rosh Ha-Shana flower seeds or bulbs that will sprout after several months (Ma'amar Mordechai 1:7).
And some learned from the Rambam that non-fruit trees too must be planted by the fifteenth of Av, because if they are planted after that, onlookers will see a very small seedling and suspect that it was planted in the shemita (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, and Ma'amar Mordechai 1:4). However, in practice one need not take their view into account, since most of the poskim did not explain the Rambam this way (Yad Peshuta); and in addition the law is rabbinic; and especially today, when it is customary to plant seedlings from nurseries, sometimes large and sometimes small, and people are not accustomed to notice the age of the plantings in the ground.

sections.title_en: 18. A Partner in a Building Whose Garden Is Worked in Shevi'it
sections.body_en:
All the laws that apply to an individual of course also apply to each one of the residents of a building that has a shared garden. And one who lives in a building most of whose residents insist that the gardener they employ continue to work in Shevi'it as usual must express his protest and ask not to take part in the payment for this, for otherwise he is a partner in all the forbidden work. And it is right that he write his protest on the notice board; but he must be careful that the protest is worded with care, preserving the dignity of the other residents, so as not to break the peace between them. And if despite this they require him to pay the dues as usual, he should pay as usual but inform them politely that the dues he pays are intended solely for the electricity and cleaning needs of the building and not for the work of the garden.

Residents of a city or a local council whose leaders employ gardeners in Shevi'it as in all the years should protest to the leaders and express this in writing, and inform them that they do not agree that the payment of their taxes be used for activity forbidden in Shevi'it.18

notes_en.en:
Some say that even when the house committee agrees that the dues the religious resident pays will go to cleaning and electricity, he still transgresses the cancelling of a positive mitzva; for in addition to the prohibition of not doing work, there is a positive mitzva that the field rest, and even if others work in a field in which he is a partner, he thereby transgresses a positive mitzva. This is the view of the Minḥat Ḥinukh 112, and so one can understand from the Gemara Avoda Zara 15b, and the Tosafot of Rabbi Elḥanan there. And in order to be saved from the prohibition according to their view, several poskim wrote that it is right to renounce ownership of his share in the garden before three people (see Minḥat Shlomo, vol. 1, 51:3; Be-Ohalah Shel Torah 3:9).
And some say that there is no benefit in this, because this renunciation of ownership has no validity under the laws of the state. And in any case, even if there were benefit in it, there is no obligation to renounce ownership, because according to the great majority of the poskim the owner of the field does not transgress a prohibition when work is done against his will in a garden in which he is a partner, as Maran Rav Kook explained (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 1). All the more so when it concerns a rabbinic law, for shemita in our time is rabbinic. (All the more so residents of a city or council whose gardens are worked need not renounce ownership of their share, for in any case they have no real partnership in the public gardens.)
But each of the apartment owners is obliged to protest about this; for even regarding a person who is not a partner there is a mitzva to protest, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your neighbour, and not bear sin because of him." And indeed, "Rabbi Il'a said in the name of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: Just as it is a mitzva for a person to say something that will be heeded, so it is a mitzva for a person not to say something that will not be heeded. Rabbi Abba says: It is an obligation, as it is said (Mishlei 9:8): Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you" (Yevamot 65b). Therefore, since rebuke is often perceived as a crude interference in another's life, and consequently is not heeded, it is a mitzva to refrain from it. But here, where he is a partner in the garden, the residents of the house have no right to be offended by him, since a protest on his part is required, on condition that he carries it out while preserving their dignity. And likewise residents of a city or council in whose gardens Jews work in violation of the prohibition should protest about this politely.
